Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild

For those that took in Mark Gardner’s demonstration last month, you were rewarded! My overwhelming sentiment was sensing that he wanted to
show/tell us everything he knows. As usual, I
learned a couple of very important things! For
those that missed it, that’s unfortunate. I say unfortunate for two reasons. One, you missed an excellent learning opportunity. I mean, if an old-hand
(read: have attended a hundred+ demos) like me
can pick up a couple of nuggets, just think what a
newer turner might garner! It’s heart-breaking to
say this, but the vast majority of the 30 in-person
attendees were not newer members – newer members have the most to gain for attending these
events. Unfortunate also for our coffers, as we lost
money- quite a lot! Is this loss worth it? In the long
run, yes as we make up these shortfalls in other
ways. For the record we had a shortfall of $1500
but with better attendance for the day-long demos,
most of that is recovered AND we can continue to
bring in talent on a quarterly basis. Without your
participation, the level and quality of our programming drops significantly.
The challenge for next month is TWO-fold. One, the
President challenges you to a lidded vase and you
can get ideas and inspiration from our upcoming
Guild Night demo by Larry Stevenson.
The second challenge is the over-the-summer collaborative exchange that Pippa Lattey is challenging
us to. Read more about it inside this newsletter.
Steve

As usual, because there will be no monthly

continue to send in articles, reports, tips, etc. for
the September newsletter.
Have a great summer, everyone!
Steve

May 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
Since joining the guild, I’ve learned a great deal
from fellow members; through conversations,
shared techniques, and the generosity of those
willing to pass on their knowledge. That experience
guided me in creating Treasure Egg, a hollow form
turned from figured maple with bark inclusions,
where the texturing process played a key role in
shaping the final piece.
Before settling on the right treatment for the top, I
experimented with different surface techniques. In
the end, I chose to use a micro motor with two
different-sized sphere burrs to create an overlapping texture of randomly sized dents, followed by
burning to accent the ridges of the textured surface. The top was then finished with Danish Oil to
deepen the color, while the bottom was treated
with Osmo TopOil to preserve its natural appearance.
A copper band ties the two sections together, created using reactive copper paint. In earlier experiments, I applied a reactant to encourage the natural verdigris patina that forms as copper weathers.
However, I found I wasn’t drawn to the green
tones, so for this piece, I opted to use the paint
without the reactant, allowing the raw copper color to complement the design.
Each project brings new insights, and this piece
was no exception. Conversations with the guild's
members and visiting demonstrators helped me
refine my approach, whether in surface treatments, finishing techniques, or design considerations. There’s always more to learn, and I look forward to carrying those lessons into future work.
Please email all Instant Gallery and President’s Challenge photos to
gallery@gvwg.ca by at least 3 days before the monthly meeting to ensure they are included in the gallery presentations.
In your email, please include as much information as possible on your
project such as species, dimensions, finish, special techniques, anecdotes, etc.
If you would like your photo to be considered as a newsletter cover
photo, please provide a high resolution photo in portrait format with a
clean background and foreground.

In September last year I was contacted by a person
who asked me if I would make a bowl for him from
the root ball of an apple tree. It was a tree that he
and his daughters had planted as a memorial to his
father when he passed away. Sadly the tree itself
developed a disease and had to be cut down ten
years later so he wanted a piece made from the
tree to continue the memorial.
The root ball had already been cleaned and power
washed when I received it but it was difficult to see
where to begin. A bit of judicious trimming with a
chainsaw cleaned things up a bit so I could begin to
see where a bowl could come out. The only practical way to hold it was to put it between centres to
start. Even at that I had to drill in a bit to find a solid spot to set the drive centre and wound up repositioning it several times.
As I turned the bowl I began to make decisions on
the shape. I often like to make bowls with slightly
closed form and it seemed like the solid part of the
root ball would suit that shape. With the bark inclusions and other irregularities in the wood I decided to just make the shape that I wanted and not
be concerned that it would result in some holes in
the bowl. It would be more a piece of artwork than
a functional bowl but turning it down until it was
perfectly solid could result in no bowl at all. The
other decision I made was to turn it straight to the
finished shape and allow the warping to be part of
the bowl rather than try for a twice turned bowl.
Once the bowl was turned I put it in a paper bag to
allow it to dry slowly. I fully expected some wood
(Continued on page 6)
Finished Bowl with Bow Ties
Apple root ball between centres
Freshly turned

May 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
movement but when I checked on it a few days later I was still surprised at how much it was moving
and some of the cracks opening up. I put some staples in to try and keep the cracks from expanding
further and placed it back in the paper bag for a
few more weeks. When it finally seemed to be
dried to equilibrium I took it out and wondered if it
was really going to be worth the effort. It had
moved more than any kind of wood I have seen,
other than arbutus, and in my wife’s words “looked
like a skull”.
Since it was a sentimental piece to someone
though I decided it needed to be finished.
After seeing Ed Pretty’s demo a few years ago, I
had made the effort to learn how to make bowtie
patches and I decided that would be the way to
handle it. I needed quite a few and there were varying sizes of cracks so I opted to make three different sizes of bowties. This was to both cover the
different sizes of cracks and to provide some visual
variety. There is a brief writeup of the technique in
our June 2020 newsletter and more detailed article
in the August 2022 issue of American Woodturner.
Once all of the patches were put in I sanded and
finished bowl. In the end it turned out much better
than I had expected. More importantly the person
who asked me to make it is delighted with bowl.

Announcing the second annual Summer Swap!
This year will be the same rules as last year. Here’s
how you can participate:
1. Bring an unfinished piece to the June 26
meeting.
It could be a rough-turned bowl, something you
started turning and set aside, or a piece off the
lathe that needs a special finish, carving, embellishment, etc. There is no need to make

nothing too big. Anyone with a midi lathe and

participant, and you will exchange pieces with

3. In September, bring the finished piece to display in the Instant Gallery.

This is for those who missed my March 2025 demo
on tops as well as those who asked for the dimensions of my tops.
Parts of a Top:
In my demonstration, I discussed the parts of a
spinning top as well as how different design decisions affect their performance. Please refer to image 1 and familiarize yourself with the point, shaft,
tip and whorl. The shaft is the long, thin section of
a top generally used to spin it. The whorl is the
widest section, where the bulk of a top’s weight
resides. For clarity, I differentiate between the ‘tip’
and the ‘point’ of a top as they serve different
functions. The tip is the smallest part of the top at
the very bottom which makes contact with the surface being spun on. The tip is the section connecting the whorl to the point.
What you’ll need:
1. Wood- While any wood can be used, for the
best results, I recommend using dense, straight
-grained hardwoods that are fully dried and stable. Eastern hard maple is my favourite, though
ash, walnut and other similar woods work just
as well. I generally begin with square spindle
stock between 1.5”-2” in width. I mill my wood
with a jointer and tablesaw to ensure squareness, and cross cut it square to length.
2. Workholding- all one-piece tops can be made
between centers, though I recommend using a
chuck if you’re planning on making two piecetops (more below) or doing more than 5 tops at
a time.
3. Tools- A standard spindle turning set is helpful,
but at minimum I’d recommend having a Spindle roughing gouge, spindle detail gouge and a
skew chisel.
4. Finishing- I primarily use solid beeswax to finish
all of my tops, but other wax based finished
work great too. I like to use Shellawax (friction
polish) on my fancier tops.
Wizard tops:
The design and name for this top are taken from
Michael Cullen’s book ‘Tops, Making the Universal
Toy.’ It gets its name because the main body of the
top resembles the shape of a wizard’s hat. Image 2
has the form and dimensions that I used in my
demo. This is a great, 5- minute project that can be
(Continued on page 10)
Image 1

May 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
completed using only a skew chisel, a touch of
sandpaper and a lick of beeswax. That said, please
use the tools that you are comfortable with. This is
my order of operations:
1. Begin with a 1.5” square, 3” long piece of wood
in your chuck and rough it just until it is round.
If your wood is not square, rough it out between centers and put a tenon on it before
chucking it up.
2. Square off the end of the blank, then from the
tailstock side, mark 1-1/8” for the shaft and ¾”
for the top of the whorl to the point.
3. Using peeling cuts with either the skew or a
spindle roughing gouge, size the shaft section
to just over 5/16” in diameter, stopping 1/16”-
1/8” before your layout line for the top of the
whorl. Clean up the surface of the shaft with
light planing cuts from the skew, aiming for
about ¼” final diameter.
4. Using a spindle detail gouge or skew chisel,
clean up the top of the whorl with straight cuts,
removing the 1/8”-1/16” of material left in step
3.
5. If desired, cut three lines near the top of the
shaft to act as grips when spinning the top.
6. Now is a good time to sand the shaft and top of
the whorl with a touch of 220 grit sandpaper,
or 150 to 220 if the surface is on the rougher
side.
7. Begin shaping your whorl into a cone by making
v-cuts centered on your last layout line, until
the point of the top is about 1/4” in diameter.
Leave a tiny flat section at the top of the whorl
about 1/32-1/16” wide. A pointy corner is more
likely to break when dropped, or could cut.

9. Continue removing wood like in step 6 until

Inception tops:
The design of these tops is based on a metal top
from the company ‘Forever Spin’ which looks very
similar to the iconic top from the 2010 movie
‘Inception’. I love them for their simplicity and how
smoothly they spin. To turn these tops, I recommend that you use a roughing gouge, a spindle
gouge (1/2” or 3/8”) and optionally a skew chisel.
Image 3 has the form and dimensions I used in my
demo, and this is my order of operations:
1. Start with a 1.5” square, 3” long piece of wood
and rough it round as with the previous top.
2. Square of the end of the blank, then from the

tailstock side, mark ½” for your tip and point,
1/8” for your whorl and 1” for your stem.
3. Starting from the end of the blank, cut small
half-coves moving towards the bottom of your
whorl, creating a small point at the end. This
top is turned with the point facing out so that
you can make a finer, more centered point.
4. Cut a line for the top of your whorl, then do a
small planning cut to clean up the edge of your
whorl. Sand the tip and whorl of the top at this
point. It’s best to sand before cutting the stem
as this helps to keep the piece balance. If you
sand after the stem is cut, the top will tend to
spin unevenly during sanding, leading to a disbalanced top.
5. Shape the top’s stem by cutting a half cove on
the top side of the whorl. I generally aim for a
3/16” diameter stem. Sand the stem at this
time.
6. Optional: Cut three lines into the top of the
stem to act as grips.
7. Colour, wax and buff the top at this point.

8. Either part the top off using a thin parting tool,
or cut it free using a skew chisel.
Colouring tops:
There are hundreds of ways to colour wood, but I
have found none more convenient or more effective for tops than simple sharpies. I like to use
them on wood that has been sanded to 220 grit
before sealing with solid beeswax and then buffing.
This produces vibrant colours with a smooth and
lightly glowing finish. I recommend primarily using
darker, saturated colours as I’ve found that anything too light or pastel does not show up well on
wood. I also recommend primarily colouring endgrain, rather than side grain, as I find that sharpie
lines on side grain tend to bleed quite a bit and
lose most of their crisp definition. When colouring
with sharpie, slow your speed to about 300RPM to
avoid burning the tips of your markers and to allow
you to do spiral colours.
Wood choice:
While any relatively dense wood will work well,
with smaller tops like these, denser is better.
Closed, straight-grain woods like maple and cherry
are ideal, though I’ve made many wonderful tops
from open grain woods like oak and ash as well. My
favourite material for tops is Eastern hard maple as
it’s a dense, stable wood that takes colour well.
I hope that this guide helps you to get started with
making tops. They’re a great way to practice
woodturning fundamentals and have a great time
doing so. If you do get around to turning some of
the tops in this guide, please feel free to share photos with me at: oakidokiwoodworks@gmail.com
and thank you so much for reading!

Laying out and preparing the blank
•
Start with blank minimum 3”x 3”x 2 inches
longer than required for mechanism.
•
Lay out points for multi-axis turning on either
end.
•
Rough down to 3” diameter.
•
Caliper to 1 5/8” diameter where mill body will
meet the top knob. Expand calipered area to
about ½” length.
Multi-axis turning
•
Mount clockwise end on head-stock side in position 1 with counter-clockwise end on tailstock
side in position 2.
•
Turn the body portion using calipered section
as a stop mark on one end. Leave enough for
minimum ¼” wall thickness on bottom end.
•
Proceed in order:
•
The result will be a clockwise twist on the body
and counterclockwise twist on the knob. This is
with knob end toward the headstock with
clockwise axis order. To get the opposite effect
use the counterclockwise end for the knob, still
facing the headstock.
Parting off
•
When finished multi-axis turning mount back
between centers.
•
Turn a tenon on either end. Form a tenon from
the calipered portion done earlier that will be
used to hold the body of the mill from that end.
•
Mount in chuck from knob end.
•
Part body off from knob leaving the tenon on
the body.
•
Set aside the mill body and clean up the bottom
of the knob.
Drilling and jam chuck for knob
•
Drill a 7/8” hole 1 ¼” deep in the knob.
•
Use grooving tool to make a notch for mechanism clips.
•
Sand bottom before proceeding.
•
Remove knob and put a piece of scrap in the
chuck for making a jam chuck.
•
Rough to round.
•
Caliper a tenon slightly over-sized for the hole
in the knob.
•
Trial & error pare it down and test fit until knob
fits on snugly.
•
Using tailstock for support, as much as possible,
remove tenon using spindle gouge.
•
Sand top of knob and sides to finish.
Drilling the mill body
•
Mount body of mill in chuck from bottom end.
•
Drill 1 1/16” hole as long as possible in the top.
•
Remove from chuck and remount from top
end.
•
Remove tenon from the bottom with as clean a
cut as possible.
•
Drill sequence of holes for mill mechanism
starting with the largest and ending with 1
1/16”. Drill through with 1 1/16” bit until it
meets hole drilled from the top.
•
Use grooving tool to make notch for mecha-

Jam chucking and finishing the mill body
•
Mount scrap in the chuck for making a jam
chuck.

Installing the mechanism
•
The lathe can be used the press the mechanism
into the mill.
•
A scrap of wood held in the chuck with a hole
drilled through the middle can be used to hold
the mill parts while being pressed.
•
For installing the fitting in the knob a press
made from a wood scrap with a morse taper to
fit your tailstock and flat face can be used.
•
For installing a the mechanism in the body a
press made the same way but with hole drilled
in the middle so it only pressed on the outside
of the mechanism can be used.
•
I like to back up the mechanical features of the
mill with epoxy but care must be taken to not
get it into the mechanism. I spread it in both
the knob and the body just before the groove
so that any excess will be pushed into the
groove.

As a follow up to the recent newsletter article asking for volunteers to become Instructors in the
Guild’s Introduction to Turning, I am excited to advise that Simon Brichford and Bob Gilson have
stepped forward to offer their services. Simon will

waiting list from the Spring session.
Leading Intro to Turning classes is voluntary rather
than paid position so please join me in thanking
Simon and Bob for offering up their time to help
the Guild continue to deliver this important program.
May Intro to Spindle Turning Class:
The Guild recently held its Spring Intro to Spindle
Turning class on May 10th and 11th.
The class was lead by
our very own master
spindle turner, Ed
Pretty, with support
from Simon Birchford
and Bob Gilson, who
jumped right in to
get the feel for how
Intro to Woodturning classes work.
Terry Kennedy, Diane Prentice, John Milligan, Keith
Sashaw and Charlene Mellors enjoyed 2 days learning of making shavings with the spindle tools, in
particular “the Skew”. Ed was excited to report
that confidence levels of all participants was greatly enhanced during the class.
Participant
highlights included: how
to correctly use and
sharpen
spindle
tools, in particular
the Spindle Roughing
Gouge
and
Skew;
understanding the benefits between cutting vs. scraping; expanding skills beyond
bowl turning; and understanding how the key spindle turning elements come together to make useful
pieces. Overall participants found the class to have
a great mix of explanations, demonstrations and
hands on practice.
As always, the Guild
sends
out
a
big
thankyou to Ed, Simon, Bob and Brian
Lunt for giving up
their
weekend
to
make this class happen.

Sanding Polyurethane between coats for high
gloss
L.S.
2025-05-20 5:02 PM
Playing around with my first jug of poly and trying
to go for a very high gloss finish.
I'm using the Minwax High Gloss Rub-on poly (that
is 50-50 solvent-poly) so they won't be super thick
coats. Looking for any advice / recipe on how to
sand between coats?
Should I sand the first poly coat in 240-320ish grit
range and then move up a grit-or-two each coat?
(So 400-600 for the 2nd poly coat, and ~1000 for
the 3rd).
Or should I just stick with a high grit 400+ for all
coats?
There's no perfect recipe, but curious what's
worked for others in the past.
———————
D.H.
2025-05-20 9:14 PM
This is what works for me.
•
I don't necessarily sand between every coat as
long as it feels smooth, I sand to 400 every 2nd
coat, unless it feels rough, or there is a run.
•
1st coat usually soaks in, and if it feels ok, then
I put 2nd coat on as soon as it's dry to touch,
usually in an hour or 2.
•
Subsequent coats will take a little longer to dry.
•
If there's a run in the finish, I'll hit the run with
320 or even 220, then finish off with 400.
•
After about 8 coats, I'll sand with 1000 grit a
couple more coats, then after final coat, I'll
sand lightly with 1500.
•
By the way....I power sand on the lathe, at slow
lathe speed, with 2" or 3" sanding discs.
•
I use 2" x 2" 4 ply non surgical gauze pads to
apply the WOP, from Regency Medical on Canada Way in Burnaby, they don't leave any lint,
and are cheap....~ $6 for 200 pads....3 cents
each.
Hope this helps, D.H.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 28)

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 28
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
